claims.text: The initial CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a uniform, primarily single-phase microstructure.
The initial alloy has very low baseline impurity levels.
Adding 0.1–0.5 wt% P or S and aging at 400–600°C will cause the impurities to diffuse.
The added impurities will preferentially segregate to microstructural defects.
Relevant segregation sites include dislocation cores and coherent interfaces.
Local impurity enrichment at defects weakens or alters the atomic bonding environment.
Impurity enrichment disrupts cooperative plastic deformation.
Disruption of cooperative plastic deformation promotes premature crack nucleation.
Impurity segregation lowers the toughness of the alloy.
Impurity segregation can shift fracture behavior from ductile to brittle while the alloy remains single-phase.
Doped and aged specimens will exhibit nanoscale impurity decoration at defect sites detectable by high-resolution TEM/EDS.
Doped and aged specimens will have lower fracture toughness than identically processed undoped specimens.
Doped and aged specimens will show lower fracture stress and more brittle fracture modes than the baseline.
The undoped CoCrFeMnNi baseline is expected to retain higher toughness and a uniform microstructure after the same aging treatment.
The embrittlement effect will be most pronounced at 400–600°C because diffusion is sufficient for impurity migration in this range.
At substantially lower temperatures, impurity segregation may be kinetically limited.
At substantially higher temperatures, degradation processes other than impurity segregation may dominate.
The extent of segregation and toughness degradation may depend on impurity identity, concentration, and aging duration.
An undoped control and a 0.1–0.5 wt% impurity-doped group will be processed and aged identically for comparison.
Failure to observe enhanced defect-site segregation or a statistically significant toughness reduction is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
